title: Protect a Production Database in Terraform
intro: This is the database config that nearly got destroyed in terraform-incident-003 — and it has a password sitting in plain text. Harden it so neither accident can happen.

steps.starter_content:
resource "aws_db_instance" "main" {
  identifier        = "prod-db"
  engine            = "postgres"
  instance_class    = "db.t3.medium"
  allocated_storage = 50
  username          = "dbadmin"
  password          = "hunter2"
}
steps.prompt: Fix it: (1) delete the hardcoded password and set manage_master_user_password = true (AWS then generates and stores it in Secrets Manager); (2) set deletion_protection = true; (3) add a lifecycle block with prevent_destroy = true; (4) add a terraform block with an s3 backend (any bucket/key/region) that has encrypt = true, so state is encrypted at rest.
steps.hint: lifecycle is a nested block inside the resource: lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }. The backend lives inside terraform { backend "s3" { bucket = ..., key = ..., region = ..., encrypt = true } }. true is a bare boolean — no quotes.
steps.fake_output:
Success! The configuration is valid.

# later, a plan that tries to replace it:
Error: Instance cannot be destroyed
  Resource aws_db_instance.main has lifecycle.prevent_destroy set.
steps.explanation: Two independent guards against deletion, and no secret in code or (thanks to AWS-managed credentials) in state.
steps.why: The layers catch different mistakes: prevent_destroy makes Terraform refuse any plan that would destroy the DB (the refactor in terraform-incident-003 would have errored instead of proceeding), deletion_protection makes AWS itself refuse — even from the console or CLI. manage_master_user_password keeps the password out of both code and the state file, the exact leak in terraform-incident-006. Remember the old password was in git history: rotate it.
